source_refs.note: Demography with the Day of Eight Billion box (PDF 235-237); Figures 25.7 and 25.8 are replaced by original graphs and a dispersion diagram is added. The survivorship types, numbered 1, 1, 2 in the book, are read as I, II, III.

blocks.text: Population survivorship is the percentage of a group alive at a given age, shown by survivorship curves with survivors on the y-axis and age on the x-axis.

blocks.caption: Three survivorship curves
rows: most live to old age, then die quickly; environment has little effect
constant chance of death throughout life
very high death rate of the young; adults survive much better

blocks.alt: A graph of number of survivors against age. Type I (blue) stays high then drops steeply near the end, as in humans and many mammals. Type II (green) is a straight diagonal, as in birds, lizards and rodents. Type III (red) drops steeply at once then levels off, as in fishes and many invertebrates.
blocks.caption: Survivorship curves (original graph after Figure 25.7).
blocks.long_description: Survivorship is the percentage of a group still alive at a given age, plotted as survivors against age. In Type I (convex) populations most individuals live to old age and then die quickly; environmental factors have little effect on mortality. In Type II (diagonal) populations the chance of death is constant throughout life. In Type III (concave) populations juvenile mortality is very high, but those that reach adulthood have a much lower death rate.

blocks.text: Population growth is the increase in the number of individuals over a period of time. In the exponential model a population grows without limit at its maximum rate, by the same ratio per unit time; not all populations show it. In the logistic model the population eventually meets limits, shortages of space, light, water or nutrients, and stabilises at the carrying capacity of its habitat, giving an S-shaped (sigmoid) curve.

blocks.alt: Two graphs of population size against time. Left, exponential: a J-shaped curve rising ever more steeply with no limit. Right, logistic: an S-shaped curve that rises and then levels off at a dashed line marked carrying capacity.
blocks.caption: Exponential and logistic growth (original graphs after Figure 25.8).
blocks.long_description: In the exponential model a population grows without limit at its maximum rate, increasing by the same ratio in each unit of time, giving a J-shaped curve; not all populations show this. In the logistic model growth slows as resources such as space, light, water or nutrients run short, and the population levels off at the carrying capacity of its habitat, giving a sigmoid, flattened S-shaped curve.

blocks.text: Population density is the number of individuals per unit area or volume, such as the number of mulberry trees per square kilometre in Muzaffarabad or of E. coli per millilitre in a test tube. Near the carrying capacity, high density means severe competition, fewer births, more deaths and more pollution.

items: Random spacing: individuals do not interact strongly; uncommon, seen in some plants whose wind-dispersed seeds grow wherever they fall.
Uniform spacing: individuals evenly spaced, as when plants inhibit nearby growth or animals such as nesting penguins keep territories.
Clumped spacing: individuals in groups or clusters, because resources are patchy or animals live in groups; the most common pattern, seen in plants that drop seeds straight down.

blocks.text: 5. Carrying capacity and 6. minimum viable population

The carrying capacity is the largest number of individuals of a species that an environment can support sustainably over a long period, set by limiting factors such as food, water, shelter and nesting sites, and by predators and diseases. The minimum viable population size is the smallest number needed for a population to persist; below it the risk of extinction is high, because inbreeding weakens the population and its immunity (as in the few remaining Himalayan brown bears of Pakistan) and a single flood or forest fire could wipe it out.

blocks.title: Day of Eight Billion
blocks.text: The world population took 12 years to grow from 7 to 8 billion, reaching 8 billion in 2022. It will take about 15 years (to 2037) to reach 9 billion, and by 2050 it will be nearly 10 billion, mostly in developing regions.
